No. That idea supposes there was some kind of central point in the universe which the Big Bang radiated out from, but while that is often what laymen imagine the Big Bang as that is not how the scientific theory of the Big Bang goes. The Big Bang did not occur at a single point in the universe -- rather the entire universe was in a single point. There is no one place in the universe that the Big Bang originated from which photons are flying away from, lighting up new space. I like to think of the Big Bang by envisioning an infinitely large sponge that has been squished down extremely small and then let go. The sponge is infinite so there is no central point or border, at least none that we can see. All we can do is see there is no border in the area around us and see that the universe is expanding still, and reverse calculate that expansion back to its start.

It seems to me there are 3 possible answers to the question. 1. There is a border outside of our sight. 2. The universe is infinite. 3. The universe is finite but space curves or wraps around somehow so that if you travelled long enough in one direction you'd end up back where you started.

I like option 3 the best but as far as I know there's no proof of any answer.

I have three answers:

  1. The edge of the observable universe is our "border", since no light from beyond it will be able to reach us, ever, due to the expansion. (By the way, I think it is possible to see galaxies outside of the visible range that has been red-shifted beyond visible light. Just switching to a new wavelength should compensate.)

  2. What some other commenters said with the first light particle to travel the furthest out from the expansion point of the universe. This isn't really the border of space though, since space is proven to be able to expand faster than light. It is a border in the sense of nothing ever being able to be further from that point, though, so if you see the Universe as "everything", that would be the theoretical border.

  3. My best answer though is that the universe isn't expanding, but space is. Distances between large objects such as galaxies are increasing, but the "size" of the universe is not. The amount of space in the universe is increasing, but to say it's expanding means that it is growing into something, but Everything isn't growing into an expanse of nothingness.

If it is expanding into this nothingness, I would love to know how the outside of the universe feels, physically outside of space and time. Then again, "physically" wouldn't make sense out there.

It's less that clumps of matter are drifting apart from another and more like space itself is expanding. It's also inaccurate to describe the universal expansion as an explosion--implying that an initial burst of energy set the universe in motion, and the universe is now coasting on the inertia from that burst. It would appear that there is some energy--called dark energy--that is constantly acting to accelerate the universe's expansion. The best way to eli5 is to use an analogy. Think of space as a balloon on which all matter is resting. Now picture inflating that balloon: nothing appears to be acting on any of the objects resting on the surface of the balloon to cause them to move away other objects, but they still appear to be moving away from each other. Interesting fact: the name "big bang" was actually coined to mock the idea of a non-static, expanding universe.

As for your question about universal borders: if a boundary exists in space at all it is beyond the edge of the observable universe. Though from an anthropic perspective, the edge of the observable universe is the border. It's certainly the case that we are unlikely to ever observe anything from beyond it.
